newsitem.title: USA: Jury in Oklahoma City bomb trial set to get case.
newsitem.headline: Jury in Oklahoma City bomb trial set to get case.

text.p: The jury in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was set to begin deliberations on Friday after hearing final arguments from prosecutors who portrayed him as a cold-blooded killer and defence lawyers who said the government had the wrong man.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch said on Thursday that the jury would get the case on Friday morning after he gave jury instructions, which he expected to last less than one hour.

Jurors, who had been free to go home at nights, have been sequestered until they reach a verdict on McVeigh, who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people in the worst attack on civilians in U.S. history.

"We are now keeping you together, separate and apart from other people. You understand the reasons for that and the importance of it," Matsch said, admonishing the jurors not to discuss the case until they are formally given it.
In a day of closing arguments on Thursday, prosecution and defence lawyers pulled together the evidence the jury has heard over the last five weeks.

Prosecutor Larry Mackey said McVeigh bombed the Murrah building out of hatred for the U.S. government and rage over the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a confrontation with federal agents in Waco, Texas two years before the bombing.

He portrayed McVeigh, a Gulf War veteran, as a good soldier turned sour, saying McVeigh had manned two weapons of mass destruction -- a Bradley tank in the Gulf War and a Ryder truck used to carry the bomb.
"The truck crawled to a stop in front of the Murrah building on that morning, right in front of children and women and men, and then Timothy McVeigh ran away," he said.
McVeigh, 29, has pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy charges. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

In Oklahoma City on Thursday, Oklahoma County District Attorney Robert Macy said that if McVeigh was acquitted of the federal charges, he would immediately request that he be kept in custody to face state murder charges there.

"We would go ahead and file a detainer on him and also file our charges against him," Macy said. In Denver, McVeigh is charged only with the deaths of eight federal agents, but Macy has pledged to prosecute McVeigh for all 168 deaths if the federal case fails.

Mackey painted the bombing as a premeditated, cowardly attack and said that the occupants of the Murrah building were innocent people and not the "storm troopers" that a prosecution witness had said McVeigh believed them to be.

"The 19 children that died that morning were not storm troopers that Timothy McVeigh had said must die ... because of their association with an Evil Empire," Mackey said. "They were bosses and secretaries ... They were blacks; they were whites; they were mothers; they were daughters; they were fathers and sons. They were a community."
"So who are the real patriots and who is the traitor?" he said, turning around the beliefs of McVeigh who allegedly hated the federal government.
Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones also gave a strong closing argument, saying: "I believe the evidence suggests ... the bomber of the Murrah building died."
Jones has argued that an unidentified leg found in the rubble of the Murrah building belonged to the bomber.

Jones poured scorn on several areas of the prosecution case and attacked the credibility of the government's star witnesses, Lori and Michael Fortier, former friends of McVeigh who testified that he told them in advance of his plans to blow up the federal building.

Another defence attorney, Christopher Tritico, slammed FBI forensic testing on evidence in the case, asking how the FBI found ammonium nitrate crystals on a piece of the Ryder truck, when it had been blasted apart and rained on.
The prosecution says ammonium nitrate was a key component of the bomb.

Borrowing a phrase from the O.J. Simpson murder trial, in which the former football star was found not guilty of killing his ex-wife and her friend, Tritico accused the FBI of a "rush to judgment" and of making the evidence fit their theory.
